planting.note: Plant container-grown palms in spring once soil has warmed; Guihaia argyrata is native to shaded limestone karst forests of Guangxi, China and northern Vietnam and tolerates brief dips into the mid-to-upper teens F once established. Growth is extremely slow, especially in its first several years. Site in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil with consistent shade; avoid waterlogging.

directions: Plant in deep to dappled shade in well-drained, humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline soil, ideally mimicking the limestone forest floor this species inhabits in the wild. Guihaia argyrata is a clustering dwarf fan palm forming slow-spreading clumps of slender canes topped with deeply divided palmate leaves that are green above and strikingly silvery-white underneath, a trait that catches light beautifully when the plant is sited where breezes lift the leaves. It is one of the few truly cold-hardy fan palms small enough for understory planting rather than full-sun landscape use, filling a niche similar to Rhapis but with better documented cold tolerance for protected Gulf Coast gardens. Mulch heavily and avoid disturbing the root zone, since this species resents transplanting and recovers slowly from root damage.

planting.note: Plant in spring after risk of hard freeze passes. Guihaia grossefibrosa shares its sister species' limestone-forest origin in Guangxi, China and similar cold hardiness once clumps are well established, but is distinguished by coarse, persistent brown fiber at the leaf bases rather than silvery leaf undersides. Extremely slow to establish.

directions: Site in deep to dappled shade in well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil over a cool root zone, matching the limestone karst forest floor where this species naturally grows alongside Guihaia argyrata in southern China and northern Vietnam. It forms slow-growing clumps of thin canes clothed in coarse, shaggy brown leaf-sheath fiber, with deeply divided fan leaves that are green on both surfaces, giving it a rougher, more textural look than its silver-backed relative. As one of the few cold-hardy understory fan palms available to collectors, it suits a sheltered woodland bed beneath mature canopy in protected zone 8b-9a gardens. Avoid root disturbance once planted, since recovery from transplant shock is slow.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions or juveniles in late spring once nights stay reliably above 55F. Rhapis subtilis is native to limestone forest understory in Thailand and Laos and is noticeably more cold-sensitive than the widely grown Rhapis excelsa, so Gulf Coast gardeners should treat it as a container or courtyard patio palm.

directions: Grow in deep, humid shade in rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil or a loose, bark-based container mix. Rhapis subtilis is a lesser-known clustering lady palm valued by collectors for its notably thin, delicate leaflets and finer overall texture compared to the common Rhapis excelsa, giving it a more graceful, almost bamboo-like appearance. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes into multi-caned clumps and performs best with high humidity and protection from drying wind, making it well suited to a shaded courtyard or lanai in the Gulf South rather than open garden exposure. Bring container specimens into a greenhouse, garage, or indoors whenever a hard freeze is forecast, since this species lacks the cold tolerance of its hardier Rhapis relatives.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a sheltered, deeply shaded bed or container; Chamaedorea geonomiformis is a tropical Mesoamerican understory palm hardy only to about zone 10, so in zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens it is best grown as a container or patio specimen moved to a protected porch or indoors whenever frost threatens.

directions: Plant in dense shade in rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil or a loose container mix, keeping it out of direct sun which scorches the foliage. Chamaedorea geonomiformis is unusual among Chamaedorea palms for its simple, undivided, broadly oval leaf blade with a shallow notch at the tip rather than the feathery pinnate fronds typical of the genus, giving it a distinctive, almost philodendron-like silhouette in the shade garden. It clusters slowly into small multi-stemmed clumps only a few feet tall, making it one of the most compact true palms available and an excellent textural accent for a shaded patio container or protected understory bed. Native to rainforest floor conditions from Mexico to Panama, it rewards consistent moisture and high humidity with steady, if slow, growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring near a support such as a trellis, tree trunk, or shrub mass that the stems can lean or scramble against as they elongate; Chamaedorea elatior is tropical, hardy only to about zone 10, so in zone 9a it should be grown in a large container or an especially sheltered courtyard bed.

directions: Site in deep, humid shade in rich, well-drained soil near a support the plant can scramble against. Chamaedorea elatior is one of the few genuinely climbing palms, producing slender, flexible stems that elongate and lean through surrounding understory vegetation in its native Mexican and Central American rainforest habitat in search of light gaps, rather than forming a self-supporting trunk. In cultivation it is grown as a novelty shade specimen, trained loosely on a trellis or allowed to drape over nearby shrubs, and kept as a container plant in colder zones for easy winter protection. Give it consistent moisture and high humidity, and avoid any direct sun, which it cannot tolerate.

planting.note: Plant in a large container or an especially sheltered, humid shade bed in late spring; Licuala ramsayi is native to tropical North Queensland rainforest and is reliably hardy only to about zone 10b-11, so Gulf Coast zone 9a growers should treat it strictly as a protected patio or greenhouse specimen.

directions: Grow in deep, humid shade in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil, sheltered from both direct sun and drying wind, which quickly scorch and shred its foliage. Licuala ramsayi produces one of the most dramatic leaves of any palm: a nearly circular, deeply pleated fan up to several feet across on a solitary trunk, earning it a place among specialist palm collectors as a premier shade and container specimen. Young plants are especially shade-dependent and slow-growing, often spending years as an impressive understory container plant before any trunk forms. Keep humidity high and soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, and expect seed germination to be slow and improved greatly by using only fresh seed.
